review:
Remember Sim City? The game where you take an empty landscape, and slowly but surely transform the area, from a small town, to a gigantic Metropolis?

Picture all of that but instead of a landscape, it's a Carribean Island. Instead of turning a small town into a Metropolis, you're turning a third world Banana Republic, into a competent, capable nation, able to compete with the bigger world powers during the Cold War.

This is what Tropico is.


Tropico 4 is the fourth installment, in a line of City Management/Political Play/Strategy games, that has existed since the very early 2000s. Aside from certain notable additions, the major gameplay, and most of the models and graphics, are recycled from Tropico 3. Which, while I kinda wish they did a revamp of models, I understand the sentament. The gameplay isn't broken, and the models are just visual representations of what they are. 

There are many additions to this game, some really add something to the game, others are pretty cool and add a bit, and some are just kinda meh. 

One of the major gameplay mechanics is Political juggling between Seven Factions (Capitalists, Communists, Religious, Evironmentalists, Militarists, Nationalists, and Loyalists) as well as the Unites States, and The Soviet Union. The seven factions are still around, but now there are three more foreign powers, Europe, China, and The Middle East. Unlike the Soviets and Americans, who will invade you if you're relations with one or the other get's too low, these three won't invade you, as much as remove bonuses you recieve during good relations. Somtimes during your reign on the island, you'll get noticed that something bad happened between one of the nations, and you'll have to pick a side. There are also representatives for the factions. They mostly add two things. First, a face and personality to represent the faction they represent. Second, to provide side objectives during your reign to earn respect if you've lost some. The side objectives go for the Nations too, mostly in the form of sending goods that nation likes, or donating some money to that nation to earn respect.

There three more additions worth talking about, firstly, there is a story driven campaign, a first for the Tropico series. You are Presidente, being mentored by a Generalisimo Santana, in the ways of managing a nation, and growing it Economically, treating your citizens right, knowing when to "kick the dog", and overall just staying in power and not getting killed or kicked out of office.

The second is Imports. Generally speaking, if your island is a giant rock and little vegitation for food, then you're screwed and have to make the most of it. Otherwise, you can import! Say your on an island with a free Weapons Factory to build! But oh no, there is no Iron on the island at all! No worries, just have a stable economy, and import the iron from one of the foreign powers. It'll arrive on the next ship, be proccesed in the factory, and you'll earn alot of money!

Finally, there are the Disasters. In Tropico 3 you mostly had five "negative" events that could occur. A rebel attack, a coup from your own military, a hurricane, an uprising, and a faction disaster if a faction really hates you. Now there are Natural disasters to spice things up. Now you have to worry about events you can predict (via a Weather Station), but cannot control. Things like Volcanic Eruptions (if your island has a volcano), A Tornado (or several if you're really unlucky), a Tsunami, Oil Spill, fires, and droughts. Fires from volcanos and derelict buildings can be fixed by either paying for a helicopter to put it out, or by building a firestation. I personally like these disasters, because in Tropico 3 I was such a good presidente that I never had to worry about a coup or anything like that. Now, there is something I can worry about when my island is happy.

So far I really like that the game is still easy to play in general (once you know what to do that is), and the additions are very nice. But I have some cons.

Somtimes you'll get a notice about doing something and have to choose an option. You can't exit out to check your almanac to see what it could impact and how to fix it, you have to choose, and that sucks sometimes. Also some missions in the campaign are pretty tough on you. You have to make sure you've picked the right traits for President to make the island truley yours.

I don't do reviews, so I won't use a number system, and instead list the pros and cons, and then a final statement as to wether you should really grab this or not.

PROS:

-Game Mechanics are the same, with additions like imports.
-Disasters add suspense and more risk to buildings wrecked.
-Story is fun and simple
-Characters have well drawn charicature type portraits to represent them
-Some new buildings to help out with the new additions

Cons:

-AI for the Tropicans are competent, but man do they job hop around, and they'll walk through Morder itself just to get some corn.
-Sometimes a choice won't let you check statistics to really understand an impact.
-Some missions in the campaign aren't easy.

Should you buy this game? If you like Sim City, you'll love Tropico 4, if you like Sim City, but want it on a smaller scale, you'll love Tropico 4, if you want to try a "modern" Sim City game, but EA screwed it up, then You'll like Tropico 4.

But if you don't like statistics, or the recycled models and gameplay, as well as the AI, I wouldn't reccommend it.

It's $29.99 on Steam, but I'd also reccomend you grab Tropico 3 for it's cheaper price, and they're the same gameplay wise.

Random purchase during a steam sale & one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a while. Will appeal to any fan of The Sims/Sims City or even some of the Tycoon games as it has a similar build your own city & run it feel. Good bits of humour & I keep going back to sink more hours into it. Well worth the price.

A fantastic city builder with a good sense of humor revolving aroung Cold War Era politics. Tropico's Latin American flair and soundtrack make for a shockingly relaxing experience even as your island falls to chaos and poor management. 

From humble beginnngs of a palace surrounded by shanties you take your little paradise into any direction you want? Be it communist or capitalist, progressive or strictly theocratic, Tropico allows you to build your nation as you please. The game is easy enough to make sure even new players are having fun while simultaneously giving vet players a challange with a variety of sliders and options to make your nation, economy, and poltiical scene more unstable. Combine that with the hilarious banter of your faction leaders as your island grows and Tropico is a game you can play over and over again. 

Also, as a quick note, people seem to be especially angry about the login requirement. It should be noted this was an old relic from when the game had online features like downloadable custom scenarios and scoreboards. Despite them being no longer active (the game is fairly old as of this review) the game still stands the test of time as one of the best city simulators of the 2010s.

I have Tropico 4, 5 & 6.  I wanted to like 5 & 6 more as they are newer games but there is no comparison:  Tropico 4 is the most enjoyable to play.  The graphics on the newer games are better but only slightly.  The gameplay however is vastly different.  Tropico 4 balances perfectly the guiding hand of missions building on one another while Tropico 6 missions have little if anything to do with one another.  The music in this game (which you will be listening to for hours upon hours as the game is very addictive) is vastly superior to the other games.  I rarely notice music in games but the Tropico 4's music is very good; good enough for me to want to go make some good Cuban food or some other tropical dish (Jerk Chicken).  Overall this game is the best in the series and I would recommend it over all the other games.  For what it's worth, I installed Tropico 6 recently and wanted to like it but after a few minutes re-installed Tropico 4 and haven't looked back.

You will find this kind of fun in this game. Tropico 4 is the perfect game for the "would-be-generalissimo", where you can always try [and make some mistakes, while] to command your own "banana republic". Have you ever wondered "what if" all people got the same [low] wages, all to expend at that decrepit pub on the corner? So this is your game.

In a comparison to Tropico 3, it's the same experience after all. Some areas were improved, it's more stable on newer computers, and we have some slight changes to game mechanics. The expansion "Modern Times" add a high-tech [for Tropican Standards] taste and more funny jokes to the main game. It's a must buy if you liked the original. 

Despites the derivative sense that a player of Tropico 3 can get about Tropico 4, new challenges, choices and jokes [they are plenty and really funny if you catch the real-world references] await the veteran. For a city-buliding game, it really delivers the experience of commanding the life of each inhabitant. It's a different and welcome approach in front of games with a broad scope like SimCity and CitiesXL.

The economic sphere is simple and it's possible to make a nice profit if one follow an economic chain, from tobacco crops to cigar factories, for example. In the welfare case, Tropicans are eager than most to accept dubious services, and have an inexplicable urge to visit churches and cathedrals [don't miss the joke on the Cathedral!]

If you want a middle-range priced game that will deliver some dozens of hours at a tropical utopic/dystopic paradise, this is, I wonder, the sole competitor in genre. Players of Tropico 3 will get less of it, but it is worth the price. Newcomers will easily find themselves immersed on this atmosphere. There are plenty of DLC for when you want to revisit "las islas".

Bottom line: 9/10

- 1 palace to guard your president

ATTENTION: if you buy this game buy Modern Times DLC too, it's worth of price and adds more basic elements to game.

In short: The only good parts of Tropico 4 is what hasn't changed from Tropico 3. This makes it a good game, but disappointing. I would not recommend this unless Tropico 3: Ultimate Power somehow cost more money than this, which I'd have a hard time believing is going to happen.

This strikes me as a creatively bankrupt sequel, most noticable in how they have adjusted the shaders and bloom to make all the content look different, but 99% of it is the same content as in Tropico 3 Ultimate Power and it now just looks uglier.

Speaking of DLC, there is a lot of it for this time, but none of it seems to offer any improvement to the game. The game as it was in Tropico 3 was already fairly complete in terms of options for its setting, and I would attribute the choice of what DLC to create more on marketing decisions and not creative, design decisions that would actually make the game any better. I have a hard time figuring out why else there is no worthwhile DLC.

One irritating new feature are the advisors. They don't appear to actually have any effect on the running of your empire, their only function is that they unlock the usage of policies. Tropico 3 did not have this requirement, and there aren't any new, valuable policies that would necessitate an increase in start-up cost. All in all this 'feature' is a downside-- it's one more hoop that you must jump through on every single session. If your choice of advisors meant something, this would be one more wrinkle to make every island unique, but as implemented it just makes each island take longer.

Voicework has been redone entirely for this edition of the game, but the lines are all the same. The difference is now the accents and mannerisms are much more muted, much more subtle. Improvement? I guess if you took the voicework in Tropico 3 very seriously and felt it was insensitively broad, then this would be an improvement. Personally I really missed the energetic, light-hearted and boisterous character-line delivery, and the words haven't even changed so if they wanted to be more politically correct this is a half-measure at best; a compromise that pleases no one.

If you've tapped out Tropico 3 and its expansions and just want more missions, then by all means, get this game. If you're wondering which Tropico to get, or want the most value for the dollar, get Tropico 3 + its expansion.

At first, I wanted to be a kind, benevolent dictator, in charge of my island which of course would be perfectly green, a land of equality, equal pay, a high living standard, jobs for every Tropican, a high level of schooling and a good member of the United Nations.

However, people kept complaining. At first, this was fine. Free Speech and all. But they were not working. Worse, they began to become rebels and attack the work of innocent, hard working Tropicans. "Right," I thought, "no more of that." I built guard posts around the nation to protect my other civilians and the economy which kept everyone fed and housed. After a while, the strikes became too much. "This right to protest is too inefficient", I thought, "and we just missed that freighter. We needed that boost to the economy." In a moment of Thatcher, I had the newly raised guards gun down some of the strikers. The rest returned to work. The right to protest had been removed, but people were happier as everyone got richer.

The environmentalists began to get angry. "It's too messy, too much industry, etc." I sighed. Look, did they like having money? Money to get houses? Electricity for movie theatres and hospitals? Wind Turbines simply don't do enough, we needed that gas Power Plant. We needed the jobs to keep the whole economy turning. I tried, I added gardens, I protected and grew new forests, but they continued to complain. So I stopped listening, and focused on the higher standard of living.

The U.S. came to me, demanding that I give them money, give this, give that, or "accidents can happen". But Agent Sasha instead never threatened me, referred to me as comrade and my islanders as Brothers. The Russians understood why I had to silence dissedence, and so we joined the Russians. At least they appreciated their people. The Americans... they didn't like this. But we stopped caring. We built assault rifles and using the funds from that, we built a nuclear weapon. Does it work? No idea, but it looks scary and shows the Americans that we MAY be able to blow something up. They stayed away and all was relatively well.

Now, schooling was fine, but a lot of Tropicans were starting to get funny ideas. They didn't understand that I was so strict because I was balancing the house of cards that was my economy. They had food, jobs, entertainment, a good house with fantastic conditions, they were safe from criminals and rebels and they could travel anywhere in the world (but mostly Russia, China and the MIddle East). If they had to not protest or speak against me, it was purely because I couldn't risk this going wrong. So I had to change a few things. I began to ask that schools make sure that children understood how fantastic our nation was, how corrupt the U.S. was, how our military kept us safe. A few people got a bit funny with that, but I needed to make sure this nation would continue after my death. I executed the rebels and burnt any book which said otherwise. People got iffy, but after a few years, they stopped caring. Good. Now we can continue in happiness.

Finally, my economy began to crumble. People refused to work the poorer jobs, they sat back on welfare and complained. They refused to pay the rent for better houses and built hovels on the side of roads. They committed crimes despite having social welfare. I couldn't make them work.

So, I built cheaper places for them to live, cheaper foods and easier work. But my towns were full, so I built them in another area. To support my now burdened economy, I had to import immigrants. Lots of them. A few people began to complain, but I shot them and they stopped. Now we have a high, middle, lower and underclass, which is executed often to save the economy.

However, Tropico is now making more money than ever, we're supporting every country that needs us, our people are famous for their money (when they can afford to travel), people order is perfect, there is no crime, you can go as far as you're willing to work, and you're safe.

You're welcome, my comrades.

    245 hours played.  Wow.

    For those that have never played the game before.  Tropico 4 is an island management strategy game set in a Carribean island.  Effectively you build buildings to provide your Tropicans with homes, jobs, religion, medical treatment, food, entertainment.  You have very little to no direct control over the people themselves so you must achieve your aims by building or passing edicts - Presidential orders.

   For those that have played Tropico before - there aren't massive changes.  This version has no Juanita on the radio from Tropico 3 who was always helpful in pointing out where your society had problems.  She is replaced by (unvoiced) faction leaders (who are different from the ones you can actually see, bribe and kill on your island).  Overall the game is significantly easier than Tropico 3 - no more having to repeat the same mission over and over.  The economy is generally more forgiving, particularly in the Modern Times expansion which provides some exceptionally helpful new buildings.  However intitial development is slower.  Many edicts require a government minister which requires a ministry and a Tropican with the required skills.  Generally choose the best available.  Competent ministers can bring you valuable bonuses.  Incompetent ones must be sacked to avoid disaster.  The campaign is linear.  Russia and the USA are joined by The Middle East, Europe, and China as world powers.  Another big development is natural disasters.  One of the great horrors of the game is watching four huge tornadoes descend on your island and spend a game year smashing up your carefully built island.  Helpfully Tropico 4 allows you to "rebuild" rubble so you aren't left guessing what each pile of busted masonry was before it got destroyed.

    Approaches differ.  I always tended to try and maximise happiness on the islands with free and fair(ish) elections and no-one being killed except active rebels.  Even then I'd always try and bring rebels back from the jungle with an amnesty rather than risk the lives of my gallant soldiers with battles.  Others I have heard play as intolerant dictators.

    This is actually a great game.  It requires a fair degree of patience although there is a speed up option but there is a gentle pleasure about watching your islanders go about their daily business with a soundtrack of funky Latin music (in fact EXACTLY the same funky Latin soundtrack they have had since the original Tropico).  This edition has virtually all the added missions and costumes that otherwise they'd nickel and dime you for.

    Effectively this involves you playing the same game thirty or more times on different islands with different resources, different problems, and different victory conditions.  But it's a great game and the different rules for each scenario do force you to modify your favourite strategies.

    Overall of all the Tropicos up to and including 4 this is the one I'd rate as the most fun.  People have talked about Tropico being a challenger for Sim City in the city builder stakes but that's not true.  In terms of fun, personality, and playability Tropico is clearly better.

     Buy this game.  You'll never have so much fun demolishing poor people's shacks, either torturing prisoners or exploiting them on work farms, murdering enemy spies, putting down rebellions, and bribing strikers.  And I play nice.

I remember playing a tropico game and for the life of me I can't remember which one, or when.   It was likely this game just played a year or two ago.  In fact looking at my history, I did play this one but the one I seriously tackled I think was the PS3 version of Tropico 5. 

The thing is, I had a negative reaction to the game.  I'm not sure why exactly.  It could be the controls, as this game is clearly designed to be based on a mouse and keyboard (to the point that I tossed my Steam Controller aside and played with a mouse and keyboard at a kitchen table)  It could be that Tropico 5 is just awful compared to Tropico 4.   It could just be I wanted instant gratification or I didn't figure out key features of the game because... well they're not really explained to the player. 

What ever the reason, I stopped playing pretty fast. 

So in the last couple years I've been trying to "Complete" or at least play every game I started on Steam.  That's a huge list but eventually I got to Tropico, and how was it?  

Honestly, I am absolutely in love with this game.  Well ok I have a heavy like with this game.  Love is a bit too strong.  I have a ton of minor and major annoyances, I'm still rather pissed about the lack of certain parts of the tutorial (or at least certain focuses) but overall the game is quite brilliant. 

The game plays like simcity with more focus on relationships.  Rather than just being mayor or king, you are a dictator, you can be a benevelont one, a brutal one, or anything else.  Run elections or avoid them.  Work with different countries.  In this game you actually can align with the middle east over the US USSR and Europe.  I mean that's ballsy in my book. 

While there's more of a focus on relationship, the game is really about building a working country on an island.  The missions are about playing along with very strong plot devices while still building your way.  The second mission for instance is all about making money with greed being a main motivator, you can work with the Chinese to use a new drill but if you do, there's compilations, which causes a side story.  (You can also reject the Chinese).  You can then shame or take responsibility or avoid blame.  These are all minor choices, but they change how people will react to you. 

The thing is the missions feel organic and quite well defined.   Often you have a mission such as "Export ore deposits"   You have multiple types of ore, and you can export any of it.  Over time your mines will export the ore and eventually you'll win.  However during that time you'll have to avoid problems of any type. 

Overall this works perfectly well, but there are some major issues that I really hate. 

Information panels are a mix bag.  Quite often there's information you want and can't get, or you don't know how to get.    Want to know how a factory is doing?  Well you're screwed if it's not running smoothly and even then you don't know. 

Farms are nebulous.  You wait six months to harvest your first good and then the farm should run smoothly, but for 6 months, there's not a good indicator.  Even when you do have a working mine you don't know how well it's working.  There's also not an indicator if you should put the mine over the deposits you want or next to it.  Very simple things are quite annoying.  Having health issues? You can place a clinic but unlike the police station, there's no indicator where you should place it.   Want to mine oil?  You probably have a deposit, but god help you if you can find it.   

How about education, how are people getting educated and is something missing?  Well good luck on that one.  There might be a good diagram somewhere to show if you're growing college educated adults, but I couldn't find it with a good amount of searching.  The point is buildings are very frustrating at times. 

All these are very annoying when they occur but are minor.  But god there's a lot of them and they build up.  

Now let's talk about my real problem with the game.  TIME.  There's the typical three speeds for you to choose from plus pause, but well there's really two speeds.  There's the paused time, and then there's "super fast speed" And the fact is, super fast is still pretty slow.  As mentioned before you have to wait months for many things to happen.  Build ten buildings, you have a construction crew that will move around and they are dog slow.  Hire another construction crew?  Good idea, but you have to build them and still, it's slow.  This is part of the game of course, but god I wish I could make the time go faster than even the fastest the game offers.  I want hyper speed, I want ludicrous speed! I just want some real speed. 

You basically will sit around for a minute or two often because you've already committed to different moves and now you just wait for construction to complete, or a building to start produce.  It's a bit dull to look at the map for something to do and realize the best move is just to wait.   Not that engaging in my opinion. 

The final problem I have is the game doesn't really explain what it expects you to do regarding money and other features.    If you have a negative cash flow you need to know how to get money and fast.   There's a lot of good ways to do this, but there info panels come up again.  You have to search for something that will export, and it's a bit of annoyance to go through everything and hope we can find something that will work.  Once you understand how mines, and farms work, you'll be able to easily handle this, but this should be taught in the tutorial at a deeper level than "Build buildings!"  What they do is important. 

On the other hand I still haven't figured out how not to get the environmentalists angry at me.  Need money?  Have pretty much any task? Have a  desire to do anything but sit on your butt and lose money?   They're going to eventually get angry with you.  At least they don't try to murder you at the drop of the hat, but it's very hard to "balance" when you need funds, but pretty much anything that gives you money will get them angry. 

The game does show factions well and shows you how to befriend them, but over time this information gets less useful.  It's great when the game tells you "The loyalists want a Children's museum."  But it's annoying when that old standby comes up "Too much pollution".   Too much pollution from just farms and a single mine?  Come on. 

And  one of my biggest questions and annoyances, what's the deal with the Swiss bank account?
According to the wiki it's just for "score" but that's exactly the problem, score doesn't matter in the game, why is there a decent push for it?   Why not just call it score? 

So there's clearly a few problems but I'm going to give this game the test that it deserves.  After playing this game, and spending what is likely going to be a very long time playing it.  Would I buy it's sequel?

Now assuming I play through most of this game, the answer is yeah.  And yes, I already tried the sequel once, but I'm willing to assume it was a problem with playing on console and try Tropico 5 on the computer with a keyboard and mouse.  So yes I'll be buying the sequel and as such I would recommend this game to anyone who has an interest in a slightly different SimCity.  It's not radically different, but it's fun to play and engrossing.  Two things I had trouble saying about the last iteration of SimCity, so there's that as well.

Tropico 4 is a good and bad game at the same time. It's really hard to rate, because it's a very enjoyable experience yet it manages to be very lacking in some aspects which are basically a norm in other 'tycoon' games.

The game's visuals are great, even 6 years after release. The texture quality of buildings/rocks/vegetation is sweet. Can't lay a finger on a bad thing about the sound either.

But when it comes to the mechanics and gameplay it feels like game is either not giving you enough information to properly manage your city or everything is cramped inside unintuitive menu. Sure, I can build plantations, destilleries, cigar factories farms, fishing huts but nowhere in the game can I find information on how much of each resource I currently have. I have no numbers on how much sugar I'm producing and how much is being taken to produce alcohol, why the factory is not doing well, how much food is currently being consumed etc. I can't see which part of the production chain is lacking. This is a huge downside for me, after games like Anno. There are some clues in the 'book' but it's a simple information that im currently producing enough food, welp.

You can produce power plants and yet there are no charts about consumption, production. You have to manually click on the power plant/wind turbine to see how's it doing. It starts getting obnoxious after you reach populations of 500+ where there is no time for such micromanagement.

The game allows you to allign your island towards some political views, yet there's no visual differences and anything special about doing any of the paths. Your island looks the game and people mostly behave the same whether you're full time commie or a capitalist. I wish I could distinguish communists/religious people/nationalists, not only read that they belong to these groups after clicking on them.

Yeah, each citizen has personality, political views, belongs to some group yet I can't see some more important information - how many people are unemployed, how many people work at selected education levels. I have no idea why selected citizen left his job as a doctor, priest.

Simple tutorials/information displayed when hovering over on option or more advanced charts could solve most of these problems. Yet, this is one of a kind game, and it's generally enjoyable (sometimes too easy) so I'd give it a go if you can get it at decent price.

Tropico 4 is the magnum opus of the Tropico franchise. It has the best gameplay, graphics, story and characters of the whole franchise. This game took the torch from Tropico 3 and made everything absolutely better. The soundtrack is amazing and gives you the Caribbean immersion you need to rule the proud nation of Tropico. The interface is clean and to the point, and the game communicates very well to the player what he is supposed to do, and the colour palettes in this game are gorgeous even by today standards. Also the jokes are hilarious and never get old.

The player's avatar has a full customization and I recommend all the DLCs (even if I never cared for the Modern Times feature). El Presidente has a progressive system of skills that grant bonuses for various traits, like -10 for the cost of buldings or +20 skill for factory workers. Some of the traits can also upset factions, with the womanizer granting rapport with the frugal women on the island but not so much with more intelligent ones. Too bad Kalypso abandoned this game and due to catastrophic crashes mid-game I lost my profile three times over. With only this minor inconvenience, Tropico 4 is a masterpiece and I wish Kalypso would give this gem more love.

Gameplay-wise, Tropico 4 has many more buildings and they all function in a more fluid way and with better proportions than in its predecessor (especially the garage receiving a much needed downsizing). The most important feature added in Tropico 4 is the fast build. This command can single-handedly save your rule and get things on its tracks in a blink of an eye. Each Tropican walking on the map has an easy to follow dossier readily available with his data and preferences displayed in a very user-friendly manner.

This game introduces the best character in Tropico: PENULTIMO! The most loyal follower of El Presidente and the advisor guiding the player throughout the game. Penultimo and Sunny Flowers are the hosts of TNT: Tropico News today; the Radio that plays the music and also discusses what is happening in-game (and God, they are so much better than Juanito...). Each faction has a representative, like General Rodriguez for the Militarists and El Diablo for the Nationalists. The bipolar Cold War, represented by Embassador Crane for the US and Agent Sasha for the Soviet Union, is augmented by the inclusion of minor powers: the European Union, China and the Middle East. Each power and faction reacts to especific actions, and pleasing one always pokes another - forcing the player to improvise. Another brilliant idea implemented in this game is the addition of mini-challenges throughout the gameplay, making it very dynamic as you always have something to do; this is particularly fun during the campaign.

Tropico 4 has a 20-mission campaign in 10 maps and, unlike its predecessors, the story is a continuous journey with recurring characters and a poignant ending. You start under tutelage of Generalissimo Santana, a well established "old timer" dictator in the vicious Caribbean political arena. The first missions are basic tutorials to get the player used to basic flow of the game: making farms, mining, understanding the factions and how to deal with the Tropican people. Along the way you get to work with allies and to win disputes with antagonists, like Brunhilde Van Hoof of the United Nations. The stories and dialogs are hilarious and go very well with the game and its atmosphere, with some missions so fun you just have to play them again - but the bread and butter of Tropico 4 remains in its sandbox format. Rule as much as you want, anyway you want it. The fun with this game is garanteed.

Tropico 4 is a game I have immensely fond memories of, having spent a lot of time playing it back in high school. This year, I came back to the franchise, and it was like wrapping myself in a warm, cozy blanket. Partly from nostalgia, of course, but partly just because this game is ridiculously relaxing - and a large part of that is from how *easy* it is.

If you're not looking for a ramble, and just want a quick review: get this game. It's popular for a reason, it's cheap, it's a very easy city builder with tons of charm. The graphics are pleasant but simple enough this game will probably run fine on a laptop.

If you ARE looking for a ramble, WELL! You came to the right hyena.
In playing this side-by-side with 5, I found that Tropico 4 is a game of much smaller scale, even though it FEELS bigger to me. The game is pretty tightly focused, without a lot of extra mechanics to get in your way, and seems to just set you down and say have fun. I wanted to try 3 again, as I remembered it being more challenging for some reason, but I couldn't get it to run on my computer without crashing often. Ah well.

The campaign is charming, but ultimately pretty easy, with only two levels that really gave me any issue and only one I actually lost. This is because there's usually no time limit or particular rush to get things done; there are a lot of unique level-by-level events that I feel like are enough fun to make the campaign worth trying, but you can basically set up some mines and farms, get a factory, and then coast until the level is over. The notable exception is the final level, which demands you get a strong economy set up QUICKLY, which felt frustrating after how generous the rest of the game was. There wasn't a whole lot of prep for that!

So, for me, I'd say this is a sandbox-focused game. And it's really not hard once you know the basics of moneymaking and juggling factions, which sounds WAY scarier than it really is. You're generally drowning in money after an hour or so, and can spend more of those hours just tinkering and building a cute little society for your people. There's lots of abilities for being a cruel, heartless dictator, but I don't find they need much use. If you're having to rig elections, your economy is probably in the gutter, or you've completely forgotten your people need to eat food now and then.

The Modern Times DLC is very fun, but I was surprised by how much of a love-hate relationship I ended up having. It adds so much that it's also an easy recommend, but the timeline is kind of a double edged sword. It's a much, much better implementation than the research system 5 tried to build, with the caveat that old buildings are outright replaced by the new ones instead of it being additive. This means that stuff like armories can't be built after SWAT is invented, and marketplaces and restaurants are quickly replaced by 'superior' improvements. While the supermarket is admittedly a solid upgrade to food quality it's also ten times as costly, and the ship restaurant doesn't really fit into my aesthetic while also not having the tiny footprint of the old one. In fact, I found myself RUSHING to lay out future residential areas, solely to plop marketplaces, cabarets, and restaurants. The transition from a grungy, run down banana republic to a glitzy, shining jewel of the caribbean is fun, but I really wish it wasn't restrictive like that. I have a soft spot for the crappy buildings and like a mixture of old districts and new, so it doesn't gel with my visual-focused style of play.

Oh yeah, a minor thing is that all the characters you interact with are caricatures - they're all larger than life and just a lot of fun to listen to, easily one of the best lil features of this game is the radio interludes. I do think a few of them come across as a bit racist, though. Boiling down nations to their stereotypes works really well when they're extremely familiar (the blowhard US politician, communist firebrand, sultry agent, etc) and not so hot when they're the kind of stereotype you'd see in WW2 propaganda.

These are just minor quibbles and thoughts I had after like, a two week hyperfixation. There are lots and lots of clunky things here that weren't implemented well, but the game is bright, fun, easily readable, and relaxing, even without the lure of nostalgia. 26 of my ~100 hours at time of writing are from the last two weeks.

If you haven't played the series yet, and you have any interest in the city-building type of game, it's definitely worth a look.  

Compared to a game like SimCity, Tropico is more mission-focused.  Islands have specific resources to exploit or ignore, and the infrastructure required for some industries means it's easier to focus entirely on one or two industries than it is to spread your resources around.  Tourism islands rely upon good press and expensive attractions bleeding visitor wallets dry, while farming or mining and industry can make for a relatively more stable economy (if one subject to the whims of international prices) but also require far more effort put into educating and housing the populace.  

Also unlike SimCity, unhappiness is a much greater direct threat to your Presidential persona.  Especially early on, you'll be short on food, housing, healthcare, churches, and schools, and extremely short on resources to fulfil those needs.  In the interim, you've got a rebellion fomenting if you don't jury-rig a working city on the double.  Inversely, like with many of these types of games (like the older Pharaoh or Caeser games) once your miniature city starts working at all, you're in the clear, and there are rarely any real threats.  (Although now natural disasters can strike, as well as things like superpower conflicts, which make for late-game threats that Tropico 3 didn't have.) 

You can play any level past completion of the objective, so you can just keep going until you have an island completely packed to the brim with bustling economic activity, and have money coming out the ears, if you so choose.

Tropico 3 is an important comparison to make because... there aren't really that many changes from Tropico 3.  Tropico 3 is cheaper, has the *EXACT SAME ENGINE, GRAPHICS, AND VOICES* and most of the mechanics are unchanged.  You might consider getting 3 first.  The differences are in disasters and mini-quests that pop up mid-mission, which DO keep the game feeling a little fresh, but if you're not certain on the series, but Tropico 3 on sale to test-drive the series.  

Tropico 5 is out now, but unless you know you want it, it's probably worth waiting for all the changes that will likely be made to the base game to be made, and play 4 instead until 6 comes out, and 5 is finalized.

Tropico 4: Middle Management With Better Weather and Worse Morals.

If your workday involves politely nodding through endless meetings while secretly wishing you could just banish your more annoying coworkers to a labor camp, Tropico 4 is exactly what the doctor ordered. It’s a city-builder that actively encourages you to embrace your inner cartoon villain, and honestly? It’s incredibly therapeutic.

The "Clock Out and Cash In" Routine

By the time I shut my laptop at 5:30, the last thing my brain can handle is a hyper-complex grand strategy game where I need to memorize a wiki page just to survive the tutorial. I just want to sit back, listen to some ridiculously catchy brass music, and quietly embezzle government funds.

The beauty of Tropico 4 is the pacing. It’s incredibly easy to pick up. You can fire it up for half an hour, order the construction of a cigar factory, mysteriously "disappear" a protest leader, and close out the game feeling surprisingly accomplished. But it also has that sneaky addictive quality. You log in to build a few farms, and suddenly it’s 1 AM, the USSR is threatening an embargo, a hurricane just leveled your commercial district, and you are sweating over your approval ratings.

Sun-Soaked Satire & Needy Citizens

The game nails its tongue-in-cheek atmosphere flawlessly. It never takes itself too seriously, which is a breath of fresh air.

However, the political factions in this game are needier than a toddler in a toy store. You build a hospital to keep the Communists happy, and suddenly the Religious faction is throwing a tantrum because you didn't build a cathedral. You try to boost your tourism sector, and the Environmentalists start breathing down your neck. There are times when I am just too tired for delicate diplomacy. I don’t want to negotiate—I just want to click the 'Bribe Faction Leader' button so they leave me alone and I can go eat my dinner in peace!

The "Why Am I Broke?" Mystery: The Legend of the Missing Teamsters

Here’s where the game genuinely made me feel like an idiot, effectively humbling me after I thought I was an economic genius. I had this massive agricultural empire set up. Tobacco, sugar, coffee—you name it. I was ready to swim in export cash like a tropical Scrooge McDuck.

But my treasury was completely bleeding out. I’m staring at the screen, squinting at these tiny economic graphs, wondering if the game bugged out or if the global market crashed.

Turns out, I forgot to build Teamster offices. In Tropico, goods don't just magically teleport to the docks to be sold. You need dudes with wheelbarrows to physically walk to the farms and move the stuff. My entire island's economy collapsed not because of a military coup, but because I forgot to hire delivery drivers. All my sugar was just rotting in the fields. It’s a brutal lesson in logistics that made me realize I probably shouldn't be allowed to run a real country.

The Breakdown

Pros

Infectious Vibe: The Latin soundtrack and vibrant visuals are an instant mood-booster.

Perfect Pacing: Accessible enough for a quick session, but deep enough to keep you playing for hours.

Hilarious Freedom: Playing as a corrupt, incompetent dictator is a phenomenal stress reliever.

Cons

Faction Fatigue: Juggling the constant whining of eight different political groups gets exhausting.

Sneaky Mechanics: If you don't pay attention to the fine print (like the Teamsters!), your empire will crash and burn.

Clunky Info: Finding specific stats on why your citizens are mad can feel like digging through a filing cabinet.

Final Verdict: For anyone who just wants to blow off steam by running a sun-soaked republic with an iron fist, this is a classic. It’s funny, it’s relaxing, and nobody can send you an "urgent" request while you're skimming off the top of your nation's GDP.
